```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  collapse  = TRUE,

  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.5

```

autoSpectra predicts soil properties (organic carbon, clay, pH, nitrogen and
30 others) from VisNIR or MIR spectra. It uses models trained on the
[Open Soil Spectral Library](https://soilspectroscopy.org) (OSSL v1.2).

This guide covers the usual path: getting your spectra into the right shape,
downloading the models, predicting, and reading the result, including
how far to trust it.

```{r load}
library(autoSpectra)
```

## The four model families

Each spectral domain has two families. Both are trained on the same OSSL data
and predict the same properties.

| Family | Sensor | Method | Prediction intervals |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OSSL_VisNIR`        | VisNIR, 350–2500 nm | masked soilVAE | not yet |
| `OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist` | VisNIR, 350–2500 nm | Cubist + PCA(120) | yes |
| `OSSL_MIR`           | MIR, 600–4000 cm⁻¹  | masked soilVAE | not yet |
| `OSSL_MIR_Cubist`    | MIR, 600–4000 cm⁻¹  | Cubist + PCA(120) | yes |

```{r registry}
names(model_registry)
get_family("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist")$citation
```

- **Cubist + PCA** replicates the method of Safanelli et al. (2025). It is
  the family validated on held-out datasets (see *How far to trust the
  predictions*) and the only one that returns prediction intervals. For a
  full-range instrument, start here.
- **The masked soilVAE** is built for instruments that cover only part of the
  range, such as handheld NIR units. It learns to predict from whatever bands
  are present.

## Your spectra

`predict_soil()` takes a data frame with:

- a `Soil_ID` column, and
- one numeric column per band, **named by its wavelength (nm) or wavenumber
  (cm⁻¹)**: `"350"`, `"352"`, …

What the values should be:

- **VisNIR:** reflectance, as a fraction (0–1) or a percentage (0–100). The
  package converts it to absorbance itself.
- **MIR:** absorbance.

You do not need to match the model's band spacing or range. Spectra are
resampled to the model's grid automatically.

Here are two small synthetic data sets standing in for real measurements. One
is from a full-range laboratory instrument, the other from a handheld unit
covering 908–1676 nm.

```{r synthetic}
set.seed(1)
make_spectra <- function(wl, n, prefix) {
  M <- t(vapply(seq_len(n), function(i)
    0.25 + 0.1 * i / n + 0.05 * sin(wl / 180) -
      0.08 * exp(-((wl - 1900) / 60)^2) +
      rnorm(length(wl), sd = 0.002),
    numeric(length(wl))))
  df <- data.frame(Soil_ID = sprintf("%s_%02d", prefix, seq_len(n)), M,
                   check.names = FALSE)
  names(df)[-1] <- as.character(wl)
  df
}

lab      <- make_spectra(seq(350, 2500, by = 2), n = 5, prefix = "lab")
handheld <- make_spectra(seq(908, 1676, by = 6), n = 5, prefix = "micro")

lab[1:3, 1:5]
```

```{r plot-spectra}
plot_spectra(lab, family = get_family("OSSL_VisNIR"),
             title = "Synthetic full-range VisNIR spectra")
```

### How partial coverage is handled

When your instrument covers only part of the model's range, the bands it does
not measure become missing after resampling. A **coverage mask** records which
bands are real:

```{r coverage}
fam <- get_family("OSSL_VisNIR")
wl  <- get_wavelengths(handheld)
X   <- resample_to_grid(as.matrix(handheld[, wl$cols]), wl$wl, fam$wavegrid)

mask <- mask_from_coverage(X)
c(model_bands = ncol(mask), measured_bands = sum(mask[1, ]))
```

The handheld unit fills 385 of the model's 1,076 bands. The masked soilVAE
standardises each spectrum using only those bands (`apply_snv_masked()`)
and was trained with random band dropout, so it expects gaps like this.
The Cubist family has no such mechanism. Use it with instruments that
cover the full range.

A row with no measured bands at all carries no information, and should never
reach a model:

```{r has-coverage}
has_spectral_coverage(mask)
```

## Download the models

The trained models are published on
[Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19004686). You download them once.
They are stored under `models/`, or wherever
`options(autoSpectra.model_dir = ...)` points.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
download_ossl_models("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist")   # one family
download_ossl_models()                       # all four

models_available()
```

The soilVAE families also need a working Keras installation. The Cubist
families need only the `Cubist` package.

```{r keras, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("keras3")
keras3::install_keras()
```

## Predict

```{r predict, eval = FALSE}
my_spectra <- readxl::read_excel("my_visnir_spectra.xlsx")

pred <- predict_soil(my_spectra, "OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist",
                     properties = c("oc", "clay.tot", "ph.h2o"),
                     with_pi    = TRUE)
format_predictions(pred)
```

The result has one row per sample and one column per property, in the
property's original units. Use `property_label()` to look up a unit:

```{r labels}
sapply(c("oc", "clay.tot", "ph.h2o"), property_label)
```

With `with_pi = TRUE`, the Cubist families add `<property>_lo` and
`<property>_hi` columns. They give a 68% prediction interval by default; set
it with `confidence =`. The intervals are conformal and scaled to each
sample, so samples the model finds harder get wider intervals.

### Check the applicability domain

A prediction is only as good as the model's familiarity with the spectrum.
`predict_applicability()` flags samples that fall outside the training
data:

```{r ad, eval = FALSE}
ad <- predict_applicability(my_spectra, "OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist", prop = "oc")
head(ad)              # score, threshold, in_domain
plot_applicability(ad)
```

The Cubist families use the Q-statistic: the spectral residual left after
projecting onto the 120 principal components. The soilVAE families use the
Mahalanobis distance in the latent space. Either way, treat out-of-domain
predictions with caution, whatever the interval says.

## How far to trust the predictions

The number that matters is how a model does on soils from a source it never
saw, not on a random sample of its own training data. We measure this
with **leave-one-dataset-out (LODO)** validation: each OSSL contributing
dataset is held out in turn.

Weighted R² under LODO, Cubist families:

| Property | VisNIR | MIR |
|---|---|---|
| Organic carbon (`oc`)  | 0.57  | 0.81 |
| Total nitrogen (`n.tot`) | −4.34 | 0.68 |
| pH in water (`ph.h2o`) | 0.48  | 0.76 |
| Clay (`clay.tot`)      | 0.43  | 0.13 |

A random 80/20 split of the same data gives R² 0.83–0.99 for every one of
these. That gap is the difference between predicting soils like the
training data and predicting soils from a new source. Expect the LODO
figures when your samples come from a region or laboratory that is not in the
OSSL. VisNIR nitrogen fails badly on one held-out dataset, which is what
drives its negative R². Clay from MIR also transfers poorly.

The README has the full tables with RMSE, CCC and the comparison against
Safanelli et al. (2025).

### Why predictions cannot explode

Organic carbon, nitrogen and most other concentrations are modelled on a
`log1p` scale and transformed back with `expm1()`. That inverse is
exponential: a modest error on the log scale becomes an enormous one in
original units. For this reason, autoSpectra bounds every prediction to
the range the model was calibrated on before transforming back:

```{r bounded}
# A model calibrated on organic carbon between 0.1% and 30%
y_train <- apply_target_transform(c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 12, 30), "oc")
bounds  <- target_bounds(y_train)

# Three predictions on the log scale; the last is far outside calibration
y_hat <- log1p(c(3, 40, 4000))

expm1(y_hat)                                         # unbounded
invert_target_transform(y_hat, "oc", bounds = bounds) # what autoSpectra returns
```

A prediction outside the calibration range is capped near its edge
rather than extrapolated. This is not a fix for a bad prediction: the
applicability-domain check is what tells you a sample is unfamiliar.

## The OSSL data

autoSpectra never redistributes OSSL data. The published models contain only
model parameters and aggregate statistics. Every release archive is checked
by `audit_release_archive()` before it is uploaded.

To retrain the models yourself, the data are downloaded from the official OSSL
storage bucket into a cache in your user directory:

```{r retrain, eval = FALSE}
ossl_download()            # about 2 GB, cached locally
ossl_cache_dir()           # where it went

train_ossl_models("OSSL_VisNIR_Cubist", properties = "oc")
```

## Interactive use

For point-and-click prediction, the package includes a Shiny app:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_autoSpectra()
```

## Citing

```{r cite, eval = FALSE}
citation("autoSpectra")
```

If you use the OSSL data or the pre-trained models, also cite the OSSL. If
you use the Cubist families, also cite Safanelli et al. (2025),
<doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0296545>.
